headline: Malaysia's new rules make firms vet their algorithms. The state's own are exempt.
context: On 30 April 2026 the data-protection regulator adopted Malaysia's first rules on automated profiling, making private firms vet any system that profiles people. The rules rest on a 2010 law that exempts the Federal and State Governments, on the basis it governs commercial dealings.

cards.big: On 30 April Malaysia adopted its first rules forcing any firm that profiles you to run an impact check first. The one profiler they cannot reach is the government.
cards.sub: They sit under a 2010 law that exempts the Federal and State Governments. PADU, the state database on 30.7 million people, falls outside them.

cards.big: When 22.5 million Malaysians' MyKad details were put up for sale in 2022, no one had recourse under the data-protection law against any government agency.
cards.sub: Section 3 says the Act 'shall not apply to the Federal Government and State Governments.' The minister denied it came from the registration department.

cards.big: Any firm that profiles people by machine must now file an impact assessment, even on one person. PADU holds 30.7 million people on 600+ data points, and is exempt.
cards.sub: Since May 2026 PADU runs predictive analytics for 26 agencies, scoring who can repay a government loan. No law makes it run that check.

cards.big: The carve-out is a choice, not an oversight: a proposal to delete Section 3 was rejected, and the 2024 reform left it standing.
cards.sub: Two newer laws guard state data from hackers and jail officers who leak it. Neither lets a citizen see, question, or refuse how a government system profiled them.

cards.big: The government now demands of every business an amanah it refuses to place on itself.
It reads like a fire code every shop must follow, while the largest building in town, the one the council owns, is written out of the rules.
cards.sub: Private firms must vet their profiling systems. PADU and other government databases need not.

cards.big: Malaysia wrote rules to hold algorithms accountable to people, then exempted the algorithms that decide who gets help, who gets flagged, and who gets missed.
